summary:
Gyeonggi Province stands under the national framework of South Korea. Gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgical requirement is falling. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had undergone years of hormone therapy that forcing surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. The Supreme Court has also allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors hold a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court issued a final, unappealed ruling that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, awarding 300,000 won in symbolic compensation against the state.

South Korea has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation in Gyeonggi carry no statutory protection on those grounds. In healthcare the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the ground that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage in South Korea, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court did issue a landmark 2024 ruling extending same-sex partners a measure of recognition in healthcare.

Within that framework, Gyeonggi's distinctive instrument is student-facing rather than visitor-facing. The province enacted the model student human rights ordinance in 2010 under a progressive superintendent of education, and that ordinance prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. Gyeonggi and Seoul are the only two ordinances in the country that also guarantee the right not to be discriminated against on the basis of pregnancy.

As of 28 April 2024, six regional education offices still enforced comparable ordinances: Gyeonggi, Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju. The Seoul Metropolitan Council abolished the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance on that date, twelve years after adoption, after the ruling People Power Party pushed repeal following an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to the ordinance's sexual-orientation clause.

None of these student protections bind conduct toward a visitor, and no visitor-facing enforcement action, arrest or incident is documented for Gyeonggi Province in these sources. Nationally, Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent discrimination against LGBT people while noting a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society; Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are broadly positive, organised conservative opposition remains active, and no severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented.
tangentialFactors:
The ordinance at issue originated in Gyeonggi, so the province carries a symbolic weight in the repeal debate that the province's own administration has not obviously converted into an enforcement posture aimed at anyone other than schools. The Korea Times report of 28 April 2024 frames the model's origin as Gyeonggi in 2010 and records a Gyeonggi-based teacher warning that wholesale abolition of such ordinances will bring a regression to human rights in the education sector.

Repeal pressure is political and organised rather than judicial. The abolition in Seoul was driven by the ruling People Power Party council after a religious and parental campaign opened in August 2022 against the sexual-orientation clause, and the fight did not end with that vote: the Seoul superintendent began a sit-in protest against the abolition, and the opposition-led National Assembly said it would legislate a national student-rights act regardless of regional decisions. Whether such an act has been enacted is not sourced here.

Wikipedia's account of the ordinance framework describes 2024-26 as a repeal wave in which the sexual-orientation and gender-identity provisions are the most disputed. The trend runs against the direction Gyeonggi set in 2010, even though six education offices still held comparable ordinances at the time of reporting.

The national picture for a trans visitor remains mixed: no anti-discrimination statute, no same-sex marriage, military criminalisation that the Constitutional Court re-endorsed in 2023, and a healthcare system whose ministry declined to write hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients — set against court rulings in 2024 that strengthened legal gender recognition and protected restroom use.
localsOnly:
The Gyeonggi ordinance's protections are addressed to enrolled students and to the school environment, and they reach sexual orientation and gender identity as grounds of discrimination alongside pregnancy. They do not create entitlements a visitor can invoke at a hotel, restaurant, clinic or border.

The Superintendent of Public Instruction conducts an annual survey on student human rights in Gyeonggi, and the province dedicates a day to Student Human Rights Day. These are resident-facing administrative practices with no counterpart obligation on a traveller.

Gyeonggi teachers and students remain exposed to the political contest over the ordinance. A Gyeonggi-based teacher quoted in the Korea Times defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition, arguing that its removal would regress human rights in the education sector; the Seoul superintendent's sit-in shows how contested the instrument is across the metropolitan area.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Gyeonggi's ordinance has itself been amended, challenged or scheduled for repeal during the 2024-26 repeal wave is unresolved in these sources; only its 2010 origin, its content and its status as of 28 April 2024 are sourced.

The status of the national student-rights act that the opposition-led National Assembly said it would pursue is not sourced, and no date or text is available here.

Whether the sexual-orientation and gender-identity clauses have been litigated, and whether any Gyeonggi education-office enforcement action has ever been brought under them, is not sourced.

The scope of staff coverage under the ordinance is stated generally as students and school staff; the precise wording of the ordinance text is not quoted in the inventory.

Border screening, visa and entry treatment of transgender documents in South Korea, and how Gyeonggi's airports and immigration points handle gender markers, are not covered by any source in this inventory.
